properties.name: A write says what it did not recognise, so a caller can tell an extension from a typo
properties.statement:
A write that stores something the schema does not describe must SAY SO in its reply — without refusing it — so that an invented field and a deliberate extension stop being indistinguishable.

THE OBSERVATIONS ARE `fact:defect-an-undeclared-property-is-stored-without-complaint` and `fact:defect-a-property-naming-a-node-is-unguarded-while-edges-are-not`; this is the intent behind fixing them. They are ONE theme in two directions: an unknown property NAME going in, and a declared property holding a DANGLING node reference coming out.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES IT A REQUIREMENT: reflow2 already refuses an unknown TOOL ARGUMENT — `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` appears 134 times in the served surface — and refuses an EDGE to a missing node through all sixteen typed helpers, with atomicity and a size-floor test. The one hole is `props`, a free object, which is exactly where a property name lands. So the vocabulary is guarded at the type level and the edge level and open at the property level in both directions.

⚠️ THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS PART OF THE REQUIREMENT, NOT AN OBJECTION TO IT: the store is deliberately a property BAG, and open-world properties are what let a project record what reflow2 did not anticipate. So this must NOT become strict validation. The ask is a REPORT, not a refusal — hence the wording.

MEASURED: `enforcement: "advisory"` was accepted, stored and echoed back on a DesignRule whose schema declares no such property; the real field is `enforced`, a bool. The write succeeded and meant nothing, and only an unrelated gap firing exposed it.

CHEAPEST FORM, and probably sufficient: echo which stored properties the schema does not declare. One comparison, no policy change. Naming the nearest declared property is a second step — `enforcement` vs `enforced` is one edit distance, and the near-duplicate guard already does this kind of suggestion for ids.
